stories.title: Two more close calls at Sydney Airport add to safety concerns
stories.summary: It highlights a persistent shortage of air traffic controllers at Sydney Airport.
article_sentences: Two near-miss incidents at Sydney Airport on August 16 and 25 involved Jetstar, Qantas, and Virgin Australia planes nearly colliding on the tarmac.
The August 16 incident involved a missed readback of air traffic control instructions, which was not caught by controllers, risking a collision.
These events highlight ongoing safety concerns and a shortage of air traffic controllers at Sydney Airport, with at least six incidents in the past month.

Australian authorities are investigating two more aircraft taxiing incidents at Sydney Airport, adding to a string of near misses and other mistakes on the tarmac that have raised concerns about safety.
Early on Aug 25, a Jetstar plane that was leaving its gate almost crossed paths with a second aircraft that was taxiing behind it, the Australian Transport Safety Bureau said on Aug 26.
In an earlier incident on Aug 16, two recently landed Qantas Airways Ltd and Virgin Australia Holdings Ltd jets had converging routes, before the Qantas crew spotted the other plane and stopped.

The Virgin jet had been told by air traffic control to give way to the Qantas aircraft, but the instruction wasn’t read back by the crew and air traffic control failed to spot the mistake, the safety bureau said.
The latest events compound concerns about a potential collision and highlight a persistent shortage of air traffic controllers at Sydney, Australia’s busiest airport.

stories.title: Muck-spreading: The smellier the better as farmers ask for patience
stories.summary: Farmers are asking people to be patient with the smell of manure as they spread it on their fields to prepare the land for next year's crops. Muck-spreading is the process of distributing animal manure across farmland as a natural fertiliser and typically takes place twice a year, in spring and late summer. Although "it might smell a bit", according to farmer Ben Clappison, from Cowlam, East Yorkshire, he says it is important as it helps improve the land and reduces the amount of chemical fertilisers. He says: "[It helps] to make everything a lot healthier and improve soil organic matter and really push towards more organic fertilisers rather than inorganic." Ben adds: "Our inorganics are manufactured fertilisers and a lot of raw products come from abroad. There's a lot of mileage on it, a lot of CO2 emitted in manufacturing it and it's expensive. Whereas this is coming out of the farm where it's produced." Ben, who also spreads on other farmland as a contractor, says the process is carefully mapped out using the latest technology. Manure from cattle, pigs and poultry is scooped from heaps in the fields and carefully weighed to be spread evenly. Ben also uses human waste, known as sludge and taken from sewage works, to enrich the soil. However, there are strict rules that farmers must follow when spreading sludge and Ben says he uses GPS to ensure it is only placed in the correct areas. According to DEFRA, it can only be spread on crops that cannot be eaten directly from the land, such as wheat, barley and oil seed rape.
